A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same distributional training data attribution work. Their main texts, figures, equations, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite the expanded title and reorganized presentation.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic regression, UCI Concrete and MNIST experiments, including leave-one-out, distributional LDS and influence-ranking results.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds CIFAR-10 pruning experiments with a Swin transformer and ArtBench attribution examples from latent diffusion models.

M1.justification: The distributional influence definitions, unrolled-differentiation procedure, influence-function approximation and Hessian normalization remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm 1 packages steps already present in v1; the new applications do not introduce a new proposed estimator.

E1.justification: v3 adds CIFAR-10 classification with training-data pruning and ArtBench-10 diffusion-model attribution. These substantially extend the evaluated tasks and domains beyond the retained synthetic regression, Concrete and MNIST settings.

E2.justification: The new pruning and diffusion experiments explicitly compare distributional attribution with single-model, fixed-seed influence functions. Pruning also includes models trained on all data as controls. The existing LDS comparison set—exact Hessian, block-diagonal Hessian, EK-FAC variants and unrolled differentiation—is retained.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a pruning protocol comparing model-specific versus shared subsets of 5,000 removed CIFAR-10 examples, retraining with matched seeds and evaluating accuracy and loss. It also introduces DDPM-loss-based attribution rankings for diffusion models. The original LDS protocol of 20 subsets with 10% removed remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 7 adds a qualitative ArtBench case study comparing examples selected by Wasserstein, mean and fixed-seed influence. Appendix E.3 also newly reports a comparison involving Hessian-span-projected unrolled responses. Existing leave-one-out, learning-rate, MNIST variance and Hessian-normalization analyses remain.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies 50 models for Figure 2 and reports 10 seeds for pruning and five for diffusion attribution. Pruning figures display individual seeded outcomes and averages. The retained LDS experiments still use 50 seeds and the same uncertainty-reporting format; increased repetitions of existing experiments are not established.

E6.justification: New Figures 6 and 12 report better average pruning accuracy and validation loss for distributional attribution than fixed-seed attribution; Figure 7 adds diffusion influence rankings. Retained Concrete/Tiny-MLP mean LDS scores also change: exact Hessian rises from 81.4% to 87.1%, and block-diagonal Hessian from 82.5% to 84.7%, reversing their ordering. Table 1 is unchanged.

T1.justification: The distributional influence definition, convergence and Boltzmann-transport theorems, assumptions, and proofs in Appendices A and B are substantively retained. Explicit gradient arguments and identity-matrix notation are clarified without changing the mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central framework and influence-function limit claims remain. v3's abstract newly highlights transformer pruning and diffusion attribution, while its contribution list and conclusion make improved pruning performance an explicit practical contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explanation of why fixing random seeds may not rescue classical attribution: chaotic trajectories and changed batching can move retraining to different optima. It interprets the pruning comparison as evidence that influence functions better approximate distributional outcomes. Existing asymptotic and nullspace qualifications remain.

D1.justification: Appendices E.1 and E.3 add substantial architecture, optimization, pruning-selection and influence-computation details, alongside fuller documentation of existing figures. Diffusion settings partly refer to another paper. A new inconsistency remains: E.3 describes Figure 3's lower panel as a Pearson correlation, whereas its axis and caption describe a gradient norm fraction.

R1.justification: v3 adds the Swin Transformer citation supporting the new application. The related-work discussion and positioning against previous influence-function, unrolled-differentiation and curvature-approximation research remain substantially unchanged; several other reference edits merely correct bibliographic metadata.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized around what influence functions sample. v3 rewrites the abstract and introduction, moves practical discussion from Section 3.2 into a dedicated Section 5 after the theory, adds the fixed-seed discussion and reorganizes experimental documentation.

P2.justification: v3 adds pruning and diffusion displays, redisplays leave-one-out evidence in the main text and relocates the MNIST figure to the appendix. It also boxes the existing algorithm and revises the convergence plot's legend and training-time axis, changing its label from iterations divided by learning rate to their product.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the connection between the framework and downstream usefulness. Unlike v1's mainly illustrative experiments, its ten-seed CIFAR-10 comparison directly tests whether distributional attribution improves pruning over fixed-seed attribution, reporting better average accuracy and validation loss. The diffusion case study and fuller experimental documentation broaden practical support while retaining the theory. Diffusion evidence remains qualitative, and the Figure 3/Appendix E.3 inconsistency limits clarity locally, but these do not outweigh the stronger empirical grounding.
